rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says this exegesis seeks to prevent Orientalist, Jewish, and extremist Shiite mischief, and that attentive readers will be protected from it.
rows.anchor: People who will carefully read it, will inshā’Allāh remain protected from the mischief of the Orientalists, the Jews and extremist Shiites.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says the Qur’an’s present arrangement was set by God and His Prophet, and is based on religious philosophy and divine-law wisdom rather than history, as with the Torah and Gospel.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ ān we have today has been arranged by God and His Prophet (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He holds that all Qur’anic groups are linked and each sūrah is closely tied to its predecessor; changing its placement would create a void in meaning.
rows.anchor: Every sūrah is so deeply linked to the previous one that a slight change in its placement will create void in the meanings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Within each sūrah, verses cohere under a central theme; removing even one risks damaging the sequence.
rows.anchor: all the verses of a sūrah are so closely connected to another that even if one verse is removed from its current place

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The established mutawātir reading is the one in the current muṣḥaf, and Islahi bases his verse and word interpretations on that reading.
rows.anchor: The conventional and mutawātir reading is the one written in this muṣḥaf which is in our hands today.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He interprets each verse and word through Arab usage, discourse context, and Qur’anic parallels, saying this leaves no doubt.
rows.anchor: the language of the Arabs, the context of the discourse and parallels of the Qur’ ān in such a manner that no doubt remains.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He argues that interpreting through other readings sacrifices the Qur’an’s eloquence, purpose, and wisdom.
rows.anchor: interpreting the Qur’ān on the basis of other readings is only possible at the expense of sacrificing its eloquence, purpose and wisdom.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As the group’s third sūrah, al-Ṭūr follows Qāf and al-Dhāriyāt, which establish resurrection and judgment through intellectual, historical, inward, and outward proofs; those works present reward and punishment together.
rows.anchor: This is the third sūrah of this group.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭūr shifts emphasis to punishment: 52:7–8 says the Lord’s punishment is certain and none can avert it; this threat is the oath’s complement and the sūrah’s central theme.
rows.anchor: It is this threat which also occupies the status of the complement of oath and also signifies its central theme.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–16 introduce a severe warning to obstinate Quraysh, adducing historical and universal facts, insisting punishment cannot be hastened or averted, then depicting Judgment and deniers’ fate.
rows.anchor: a vivid picture of the Day of Judgement, with a brief description of the dreadful fate of those who had denied it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 17–28 contrast believers’ bliss with deniers’ fate; God reunites believers with children raised for the Hereafter by promoting those of lower rank, without demoting those who earned higher rank.
rows.anchor: A special favour which is highlighted here is that the Almighty will reunite

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Family reunion does not reduce anyone’s earned reward; the lower-ranked are raised, faithless people cannot enter Paradise, and the Almighty’s blessings are for believers.
rows.anchor: a person’s deeds nor will a faithless person be able to enter Paradise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the concluding section, the Prophet should ignore disbelievers’ excuses against his prophethood and continue reminding people, leaving the mindful able to choose rightly and the obstinate without excuse.
rows.anchor: he should not pay any heed to the excuses invented by the disbelievers in order to deny his prophethood.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The adversaries’ verse 12 posture of pleasantries and treating truth as play is addressed in detail and silenced later in the sūrah.
rows.anchor: In the twelfth verse, the attitude of the adversaries of indulging in pleasantries and toying with the truth was referred to.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rebellious people are warned that their schemes will soon collapse and that worldly torment will precede the torment of the Final Day.
rows.anchor: before the torment of the Final Day, they will encounter another torment in this world also.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told to wait patiently for his Lord’s decision and remain aware of God’s direct protection.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) is comforted that he should patiently await his Lord’s decision

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should strengthen his patience with prayers, especially at night and in the early morning.
rows.anchor: He should augment this patience through prayers, especially the night and early morning ones.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi follows Farāhī’s account that most Qur’anic oaths substantiate a stated muqsam ʿalayh; the particle wāw here marks an oath.
rows.anchor: in the light of the research carried out by my mentor Imām Ḥamīd al-Dīn Farāhī in his Aqsām al-Qur’ān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The muqsam ʿalayh is the certain punishment in 52:7, so the Sinai oath proves that threat; Islahi renders the opening “Ṭūr bears witness,” which he finds more meaningful.
rows.anchor: the oath sworn by the mount of Sinai is meant to substantiate this claim.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭūr refers to Mount Sinai, which is mentioned in various aspects in the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: The word Ṭūr refers to the mount of (Sinai) which has been mentioned in the Qur’ān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At sacred valley Ṭuwā Moses saw divine disclosures on returning from Madyan, received prophethood, and was sent to warn Pharaoh and his people that rebellion would bring God’s scourge.
rows.anchor: It is in one of its sacred valleys Ṭuwā that Moses (sws) witnessed divine disclosures while coming back from Madyan.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Pharaoh’s destruction, God summoned Moses to the same mountain to give him Torah; later the Israelites repented there after calf worship as God shook the mountain and warned them to keep their covenant.
rows.anchor: the Almighty called him to this very mountain to give him the Torah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says Ṭūr’s layered history makes it a historical sign supporting the certainty of punishment, so it appropriately follows as oath evidence.
rows.anchor: Because of these multifarious features the mount Ṭūr is a great historical sign which substantiates this claim and is mentioned after oath.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi connects the same historical feature to the oath in Sūrah al-Tīn, saying it too substantiates the claim of reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: Thus, for this characteristic, it has been sworn by in Sūrah al-Tīn.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although some take Ṭūr as any mountain, Islahi rejects this: that sense may occur in Hebrew or Syriac, but is not conventional Arabic usage, and Qur’anic occurrences use it as a proper name.
rows.anchor: in Arabic, it is not commonly and conventionally used in this meaning.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A generic-mountain interpretation would leave the oath unrelated to its essential muqsam ʿalayh, making the oath out of place.
rows.anchor: if it is interpreted to mean a mountain, it will bear no relationship with the muqsam ‘alayh which is essential; otherwise the oath will be out of place.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi identifies the inscribed book as the Torah because it follows Ṭūr and Moses received it there; the scroll-on-parchment description confirms that no other book is meant.
rows.anchor: These words refer to the Torah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Raqq denotes thin writing parchment; the Torah’s clean-hide sheets were folded as a scroll and opened for recitation, supporting the identification.
rows.anchor: thin parchment which was used for writing in ancient times.

rows.speaker: Some people
rows.claim: Some interpret the inscribed scripture as a record; Islahi rejects this because such evidence would help in the world to come, not in this world.
rows.anchor: Some people have interpreted it to mean “record.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says the Torah reference is directly related to the oath’s claim; the segment cuts off after he begins an explanation with “Just as.”
rows.anchor: The relationship of these words is also very evident with the muqsam ‘alayh. Just as
